subject: ela
intro: These exercises ask you to look at how a short informational passage is built. For each one, read the passage that is printed in the question, then identify the organizational pattern, locate where a part sits in the structure, or name the job a sentence or paragraph does. Watch for signal words like first, because, however, and for example. They are clues to how the author put the text together.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

Making slime at home is simple. First, pour glue into a bowl. Next, stir in a spoonful of baking soda. Then add a few drops of contact lens solution. Finally, knead the mixture with your hands until it is stretchy.

Which organizational pattern does the author use to structure this passage?
items.answer: Chronological or sequence order. The author lays out the steps in the order they must be done, using the signal words first, next, then, and finally.

steps: Look for signal words that show order. The passage uses first, next, then, and finally.
These words mark a series of steps that must happen one after another.
When an author presents steps in the order they should be done, the pattern is sequence, also called chronological order.
So the structure is sequence order, signaled by first, next, then, and finally.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

The town's only bridge collapsed last spring. Because the bridge was gone, drivers had to take a long detour around the river. As a result, the trip to school went from ten minutes to nearly an hour.

Which organizational pattern does the author use to structure this passage?
items.answer: Cause and effect. The author connects an event to its results using the signal words because and as a result.

steps: Identify the relationship between the ideas. The bridge collapse leads to other things happening.
Find the signal words. The passage uses because and as a result.
These words link a cause (the bridge was gone) to its effects (a long detour and a longer trip).
So the pattern is cause and effect, signaled by because and as a result.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

Dolphins and sharks both live in the ocean and both are strong swimmers. However, dolphins are mammals that breathe air, while sharks are fish that breathe through gills. In contrast to sharks, dolphins must come to the surface for air.

Which organizational pattern does the author use to structure this passage?
items.answer: Compare and contrast. The author shows how dolphins and sharks are alike and different, using the signal words both, however, while, and in contrast.

steps: Notice that the passage discusses two things, dolphins and sharks.
Look for words that show similarity and difference. The passage uses both, however, while, and in contrast.
These words point out what the two animals share and how they differ.
When an author lines up two subjects to show likenesses and differences, the pattern is compare and contrast.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

Many students were skipping breakfast and felt too tired to focus in class. To fix this, the school started a free morning breakfast program. Now students who eat the meal report feeling more alert during their first lessons.

Which organizational pattern does the author use to structure this passage?
items.answer: Problem and solution. The author first names a problem (tired, unfocused students) and then presents a solution (a free breakfast program) and its results.

steps: Find what is wrong in the passage. Students skip breakfast and feel too tired to focus. That is the problem.
Find what is done about it. The school starts a free breakfast program. That is the solution.
The phrase to fix this signals that a solution is being offered for the problem.
Because the author states a problem and then offers a solution, the pattern is problem and solution.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

The Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean on Earth. Its surface stretches across more than sixty million square miles. The water is deep, dark, and cold near the bottom, and it is home to thousands of unusual creatures.

Which organizational pattern does the author use to structure this passage?
items.answer: Description. The author gives details and facts about one topic, the Pacific Ocean, to help the reader picture it.

steps: Notice the passage stays on one topic: the Pacific Ocean.
The sentences list details about it: its size, its depth, its temperature, and its creatures.
There are no sequence, cause, comparison, or problem signals. The author is simply describing.
When a passage gives details and facts about a single topic, the pattern is description.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph below, which is the opening of an article.

Honey bees may be small, but they do an enormous job. In this article, you will learn how bees find flowers, how they make honey, and why farmers depend on them. Without bees, many of the foods we eat would disappear.

Where does this paragraph fit in the overall structure of the article?
items.answer: It is the introduction. It names the topic (honey bees) and previews the main ideas the rest of the article will explain.

steps: Read what the paragraph does. It names the topic, honey bees, and tells what the article will cover.
The phrase in this article, you will learn shows it is setting up what comes next.
A paragraph that introduces the topic and previews the main ideas is the introduction.
So this paragraph is the introduction of the article.

items.prompt:
Read the short passage.

Volcanoes can be dangerous, but they also help the planet. They build new land, enrich the soil, and create islands. For all these reasons, scientists say volcanoes are one of nature's most important forces.

The last sentence begins with the words For all these reasons. Where does this sentence fit in the structure of the passage?
items.answer: It is the conclusion. It wraps up the passage by drawing a final point from the reasons the author has just listed.

steps: Look at the position of the sentence. It comes at the end of the passage.
The phrase for all these reasons points back to the points already made.
The sentence sums up those points into one final statement about volcanoes.
A sentence at the end that pulls the ideas together is the conclusion.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph.

Recycling helps the environment in several ways. For example, recycling one ton of paper saves about seventeen trees. It also uses far less water and energy than making paper from scratch.

What job does the first sentence, "Recycling helps the environment in several ways," do in this paragraph?
items.answer: It states the main idea. It tells the reader the paragraph's central point, and the sentences that follow give examples that support it.

steps: Read the first sentence on its own. It makes a general claim: recycling helps the environment in several ways.
Read what follows. The other sentences give specific examples, such as saving trees and using less water.
The general statement that the examples support is the main idea.
So the first sentence states the main idea of the paragraph.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph.

Many animals migrate to survive the winter. For example, monarch butterflies fly thousands of miles south to Mexico, and some whales swim to warmer waters to give birth.

What job does the sentence that begins with "For example" do in this paragraph?
items.answer: It gives examples that support the main idea. The phrase for example introduces specific cases of animals that migrate.

steps: Notice the signal phrase for example at the start of the sentence.
This phrase tells the reader that specific cases are coming.
The sentence names monarch butterflies and whales as cases of migrating animals.
Its job is to give examples that support the main idea that animals migrate to survive winter.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

For years, the city library was crowded and loud. The reading rooms were too small for everyone who wanted a quiet place to study. To solve this, the city built a new wing with extra quiet rooms.

What job does the last sentence, "To solve this, the city built a new wing with extra quiet rooms," do in the passage?
items.answer: It presents the solution. After the passage describes a problem (the library was crowded and loud), this sentence tells what was done to fix it.

steps: Find the problem in the passage. The library was crowded and loud with too little space.
Look at the last sentence. The phrase to solve this signals a fix is coming.
The sentence says the city built a new wing with quiet rooms.
Its job is to present the solution to the problem described earlier.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

Electric cars are becoming popular for good reasons. They produce no exhaust as they drive. They are also quieter than gas cars. However, electric cars can be expensive to buy, and finding a place to charge them is not always easy.

What is the purpose of the sentence that begins with the word "However"?
items.answer: It signals a shift. The word however moves the passage from listing the benefits of electric cars to presenting their drawbacks.

steps: Read the sentences before however. They list good points: no exhaust and less noise.
Read the sentence with however. It names problems: high cost and hard charging.
The word however marks a change in direction from positives to negatives.
So the purpose of that sentence is to signal a shift from benefits to drawbacks.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

A total solar eclipse is rare and amazing. First, the moon slides slowly in front of the sun. Next, the sky grows dark in the middle of the day. Then, for a few minutes, only a glowing ring is left around the moon. Finally, the sun returns and daylight comes back.

Which organizational pattern does the author use, and which words signal it?
items.answer: Sequence or chronological order. The signal words first, next, then, and finally show the events of the eclipse happening in time order.

steps: Look for words that show order in time. The passage uses first, next, then, and finally.
These words walk the reader through the stages of the eclipse one after another.
Presenting events in time order is the sequence or chronological pattern.
So the pattern is sequence, signaled by first, next, then, and finally.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph, which opens a report.

Deserts are some of the harshest places on Earth, yet they are full of life. This report will explain how desert plants store water, how desert animals stay cool, and why the desert comes alive at night.

What job does this paragraph do in the report?
items.answer: It introduces the topic and previews the main ideas. It names the subject (deserts) and tells the reader what the rest of the report will explain.

steps: Read what the paragraph names: deserts, the topic of the report.
Notice the phrase this report will explain, which points forward to the rest of the text.
The paragraph lists what is coming: how plants store water, how animals stay cool, and why the desert comes alive at night.
A paragraph that names the topic and previews what follows does the job of introducing the topic.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

Sleep is more important than many people think. Because the brain sorts and stores memories during sleep, students who sleep well remember more of what they study. As a result, getting enough rest can actually raise a student's grades.

Which organizational pattern does the author use to structure this passage?
items.answer: Cause and effect. The author links sleep to its results using the signal words because and as a result.

steps: Look at how the ideas connect. Sleep leads to better memory, which leads to better grades.
Find the signal words. The passage uses because and as a result.
These words tie a cause (sleeping well) to its effects (remembering more and higher grades).
So the pattern is cause and effect.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph.

The rain forest is full of surprises. A glass frog has skin so clear you can see its heart beating. A sloth moves so slowly that tiny plants grow in its fur. A walking stick insect looks exactly like a twig.

What job do the three sentences after the first one do in this paragraph?
items.answer: They give examples that support the main idea. Each sentence is a specific example of a surprising rain forest creature, backing up the opening claim that the rain forest is full of surprises.

steps: Read the first sentence. It makes a general claim: the rain forest is full of surprises.
Read the next three sentences. Each describes one surprising creature: the glass frog, the sloth, and the walking stick insect.
These specific creatures are examples that back up the general claim.
So the three sentences give examples that support the main idea.
